strings.name: Nicola Sturgeon
strings.role: Former First Minister of Scotland and former SNP leader
strings.summary: Nicola Sturgeon is a Scottish politician and former solicitor who entered the Scottish Parliament in 1999. She led Scotland’s government and the Scottish National Party from 2014 to 2023, becoming the first female first minister. Governing through Brexit and Covid-19, she sought another independence referendum, but the devolution framework limited the proposed legislation. After leaving parliament in 2026, she continued engaging with political issues through writing and public discussion.
strings.coverageNote: Checked through 18 November 2026. Parliament records the end of her MSP service on 8 April; an 18 August book-festival report supports recent activity. Intention to resign, actual departure and the end of the police investigation are distinguished. Other people’s criminal responsibility is not attributed to her.
strings.influence.rationale: Her long leadership of Scotland’s government and the SNP influenced UK politics through independence, referendum and social-policy debates.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and legal education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Irvine, Scotland, on 19 July 1970, she attended Greenwood Academy. The University of Glasgow confirms her 1992 LLB and 1993 Diploma in Legal Practice. The diploma is not presented as a law master’s degree or doctorate.
strings.facts.f2.label: From legal practice to devolved politics
strings.facts.f2.value: Before entering parliament, she worked as a solicitor at Glasgow’s Drumchapel Law and Money Advice Centre. Her 1992 and 1997 bids for a UK House of Commons seat failed. In 1999 she was elected to the Scottish Parliament, a different legislature.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Political reflection through a memoir
strings.highlights.h1.text: Macmillan published her memoir Frankly, listing 14 August 2025 as the publication date. It recounts her journey from growing up in Ayrshire to leading government. It is a participant’s personal account; publication and endorsements do not independently verify every contested claim.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Public discussion after leaving office
strings.highlights.h2.text: The Scotsman reported on 18 August 2026 that she appeared alongside former Finnish prime minister Sanna Marin at the Edinburgh International Book Festival and discussed the party investigation and climate policy. This confirms participation; the date is the report’s date, and later event announcements are not treated as proof of attendance.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Scottish parliamentary service ends
strings.timeline.t1.text: The official parliamentary record ends her Glasgow Southside service on 8 April and identifies her as a former MSP. She had represented that constituency since 2011, Glasgow Govan from 2007 to 2011, and the Glasgow region from 1999 to 2007.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Police confirm she is no longer under investigation
strings.timeline.t2.text: ITV reproduced the police statement that inquiries into her concerning party finances had concluded without charges. Arrested on 11 June 2023, she was released while inquiries continued. Ending the investigation was not an acquittal after trial and did not end other people’s cases.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Formally resigns as first minister
strings.timeline.t3.text: She tendered her formal resignation to the King; the government announcement confirms her departure that day. Her 15 February announcement expressed an intention to resign, with full responsibilities retained in the interim. She remained an MSP after leaving government leadership, until 2026.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Referendum bill exceeds devolved legislative powers
strings.timeline.t4.text: The UK Supreme Court unanimously held that, without modifying reserved matters, the Scottish Parliament could not legislate for the proposed independence referendum. The decision concerned legislative competence, not whether Scotland should become independent; no new referendum had taken place.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Sworn in as the first female first minister
strings.timeline.t5.text: She became SNP leader on 14 November and was sworn in as first minister at the Court of Session on 20 November. Party leadership succession and appointment as head of government were separate procedures. She succeeded Alex Salmond in leading Scotland’s government.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Takes responsibility for infrastructure
strings.timeline.t6.text: Remaining deputy first minister, she moved from health to the cabinet portfolio for infrastructure, capital investment and cities, which she held until becoming first minister in 2014. This changed her government responsibilities rather than ending her cabinet service.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Enters government as deputy first minister
strings.timeline.t7.text: She became deputy first minister and health secretary in Alex Salmond’s government, beginning her cabinet career. Official records date the start of her deputy first minister service to 2007, rather than the 2011 date in some secondary accounts.
strings.timeline.t8.title: First elected to the Scottish Parliament
strings.timeline.t8.text: She became a regional MSP for Glasgow at the first Scottish Parliament election following devolution. She later represented Govan and Glasgow Southside, continuing her parliamentary career until 2026.
